title: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (3 of 7)
hook: the third wish, the best bribe ever offered, and a boy who turns it down
carry: choose the good over the pleasant
tomorrow: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (4 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, vara: a boon for each of three nights at Death's door. Peace with his father, and the fire that leads to heaven.

There's a question people rarely say out loud. It comes at funerals, at three in the morning, in the hospital parking lot. When someone dies, what happens? Are they still, somewhere? Nachiketa is sitting across from the one being who would actually know. He has one wish left, and he asks it. What follows turns on a choice that shows up in small ways all day long: the good, or the pleasant.
screen: `THE THREE A.M. QUESTION.` → `ONE WISH LEFT.` → `HE ASKS IT.`

segments.voice: The third wish: when a person dies, there's this doubt. Some say they still are; some say they are not. Teach me this. Yama flinches. Even the gods doubted about this, he says. It's subtle, not easy to know. Choose another wish. Don't press me. Nachiketa doesn't budge: if even the gods doubted, and you say it's hard to know, then there's no teacher like you and no wish like this one. So Death tries a bribe. Sons and grandsons who'll live a hundred years. Herds of cattle, elephants, gold, horses. Land as wide as you like, and as many years as you want. Beautiful companions with chariots and music, rare among mortals. Enjoy them all. Just don't ask me about death. The boy says: these last only till tomorrow, Death. They wear out the sharpness of the senses. Even a whole life is short. Keep your horses, your songs and dances. No one is made content by wealth. Now Yama's tone changes. Many pleasures, he says, did not tempt you. And he teaches the two paths. One is shreyas, the good. The other is preyas, the pleasant. Both come to a person, and both bind. The wise one looks them over, tells them apart, and chooses the good over the pleasant. The foolish one chooses the pleasant, for the sake of getting and keeping. The pleasant isn't evil; it's what feels nice now. The good is what's actually good for you, and it often doesn't feel like much at first. Nachiketa just chose it, in front of Death.
screen: `WHEN SOMEONE DIES, WHAT THEN?` · `CHOOSE ANOTHER WISH.` · `KEEP YOUR HORSES AND SONGS.` · `THE GOOD, AND THE PLEASANT.` · then, large: `THE TWO PATHS.`

segments.voice: Picture one choice waiting for you today, the phone or the walk, the extra drink or the early night, the easy reply or the honest one, and set the two paths side by side. Feel how the pleasant pulls, and how quiet the good is. You don't have to decide; just look them over the way the wise one in the Katha does, until the difference is plain.
Shreyas, the good, the better. Paired with preyas, the pleasant: both come to a person, and both bind. The wise look them over and choose the good; Nachiketa turned down the world for his question.
Your line: choose the good over the pleasant. Both paths come to everyone. That's day two hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers use the Katha's shreyas and preyas, the good and the pleasant, as everyday language for moral choices; the passage opens the second section of the Katha.

myth: Yama answers the third question right away
he tries to talk the boy out of it, then offers a bribe.
Nachiketa says no one is made content by wealth
keep your horses, your songs and dances.
the Katha says the pleasant is evil
both bind; the wise tell them apart and choose the good.

fork.setup: Death offers you gold, long life, and every pleasure, if you'll drop your question. what do you do?
options: take half the gifts and ask later.
fork.reveal: Nachiketa refuses: these last only till tomorrow. Yama is delighted, and teaches the good and the pleasant.

original.note: Sanskrit: shreyas, the good, the better; paired with preyas, the pleasant, the dearer. Katha 1.2.1–2.

trapdoor: what you thought: Nachiketa is a boy who hates fun.
what it means: he sees the pleasant clearly, and chooses the good over it.
what a scholar hears: shreyas and preyas are comparatives (better, dearer); the fool chooses the pleasant for yoga-kshema, getting and keeping.
guess: the good, what truly serves you
the pleasant, what feels good now
a vow to give up every pleasure
recall: the ultimate reality, ground of all
the ear, the sense of hearing
